security.title: Security

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.desc: Protection from tracking and surveillance. Private email, encrypted messaging, and tracker-blocking hide your data from companies.

mfa_reminder.title: Enable 2FA everywhere!
mfa_reminder.desc: Use an authenticator app (not SMS). This stops 99% of account hacks.

passwords.title: Accounts & Authentication
passwords.subtitle: Secure your digital identity with Managers, MFA, and Passkeys.

quick.title: If you only do one thing today
actions: Install a password manager and import your top 5 accounts.
Enable MFA on email + bank (avoid SMS; use an app).
Download and store backup codes offline (photo or print).

why_manager.title: Why use a Password Manager?
why_manager.desc: Humans are bad at creating random passwords. Computers are great at it. A password manager generates and stores unique, complex passwords for every account.

bitwarden.desc: USE THIS. Free, open-source, works on all devices. The gold standard.

proton.desc: Alternative if you're already in the Proton ecosystem.

apple.desc: Apple-only fallback. Limited to Safari and Apple devices.

desktop.title: Desktop (Windows / Mac)
steps: 1. Go to bitwarden.com and create a free account.
2. Install the Bitwarden browser extension for Chrome, Edge, or Firefox.
3. Log in to the extension.
4. Turn off your browser's built-in password saving to avoid confusion.

mobile.title: Mobile (iOS / Android)
steps: 1. Download the Bitwarden app from the App Store or Play Store.
2. Log in with your account.
3. CRITICAL: Go to Phone Settings -> Passwords (or Auto-fill Service) -> Select Bitwarden.
4. Now Bitwarden can automatically type passwords into your apps.

recovery.title: Recovery & backup codes
items: Download and store MFA backup codes offline (print or password manager secure note).
Keep a second authenticator app/device enrolled when possible.
Set a unique recovery email that also has MFA.
recovery.note: Lose the backup codes? Turn off MFA, re-enable it, and save the new codes immediately.

bad_passwords.title: Stop Using These Passwords
bad_passwords.desc: If you use any of these, change them immediately:

good_passwords.title: What "good" looks like
good_passwords.desc: Long, unique, and generated by your manager. For passphrases, combine 4–5 random words.

questions.prompt: What’s the biggest risk of using SMS for MFA?
options: SIM swap attacks can steal your number
questions.correct: SIM swaps are common; use app or hardware MFA instead.
questions.explainer: SMS relies on carriers; attackers can hijack your number.

questions.prompt: Best place to store backup codes?
options: Password manager secure note or printed offline
questions.correct: Store them offline or in a secure note, not in plain email/photos.
questions.explainer: Email/photos are easy targets if the account is compromised.

questions.prompt: How many accounts should share the same password?
questions.correct: Reuse = chain breach. Use unique, manager-generated passwords.
questions.explainer: One breach shouldn’t open every other account.

mfa.title: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
mfa.subtitle: The single most important setting to enable.
mfa.intro: MFA adds a second lock to your account. Even if a hacker steals your password, they can't get in without the second key.

sms.title: SMS (Text Messages)
sms.desc: AVOID. Vulnerable to SIM swapping attacks where hackers steal your phone number.

apps.title: Authenticator Apps
apps.desc: USE THIS. Scan a QR code, get a new 6-digit code every 30 seconds. Works offline. See 2FAS below.

hardware.title: Hardware Keys (YubiKey)
hardware.desc: Maximum Security. A physical USB key you plug in. Phishing-proof but costs $50+.

biometrics.title: Biometrics
biometrics.desc: Fingerprint or FaceID. Convenient, often used as a second factor on mobile devices.

app_recommendation.desc: 2FAS is free, open-source, works on iOS and Android. No account needed. Syncs between devices via iCloud/Google backup. Simple, no bloat.

bitwarden_advanced.title: Advanced Bitwarden Features
bitwarden_advanced.otp: Bitwarden Premium can generate MFA codes (TOTP) just like Authy. This makes logging in faster (auto-fill everything).
bitwarden_advanced.passkeys: Bitwarden can now store Passkeys, allowing you to sync them across all your devices, not just Apple or Google ones.

quick_actions.title: Fast wins
items: Email, bank, and cloud storage should always have MFA with an app or hardware key.
Avoid SMS unless no other option. If forced to use SMS, set a PIN with your carrier to reduce SIM-swap risk.
Store backup codes offline and label them by service.

gmail.title: Gmail MFA Setup
steps: Go to 'Manage your Google Account' -> 'Security'.
Click '2-Step Verification' -> 'Get Started'.
Choose 'Authenticator App' (Recommended). Avoid SMS.
Scan the QR code with your 2FA app (2FAS, Raivo).
Enter the 6-digit code to verify.
CRITICAL: Download Backup Codes and store them offline.

proton.title: Proton Mail MFA Setup
steps: Go to Settings -> 'Account and password'.
Click 'Enable two-factor authentication'.
Scan QR code with your authenticator app.
Enter the 6-digit code.
SAVE the recovery codes shown. This is mandatory.

passkeys.title: Passkeys: The Future
passkeys.desc: Passkeys replace passwords with cryptographic keys stored on your device. You login with FaceID or TouchID.
passkeys.setup: To setup on Google: Go to g.co/passkeys and click 'Use passkeys'.
notes: Passkeys work best when you’re signed into the same account on phone + laptop (Apple ID, Google, or Microsoft).
On shared computers, stick to passwords + MFA instead of passkeys.
You can export passkeys to move between ecosystems (e.g., to Bitwarden).

browsing.title: Safe Browsing
browsing.subtitle: Take back your privacy. Block trackers and ads.

extensions.title: Essential Extensions
extensions.intro: Install these on every browser you use.

ublock.title: uBlock Origin
ublock.desc: The best ad and tracker blocker. Uses very little memory.

privacy_badger.title: Privacy Badger
privacy_badger.desc: Learns to block invisible trackers automatically. By EFF.

quick_settings.title: Copy/paste settings to harden any browser
items: Disable third-party cookies.
Turn on HTTPS-Only mode.
Block pop-ups and auto-play media.
Turn off telemetry/usage reporting.

browsers.title: Secure Browsers
browsers.brave: USE THIS for daily browsing. Blocks ads & trackers out of the box. Fast.
browsers.firefox: Good alternative. Requires manual hardening for best privacy.
browsers.tor: For maximum anonymity only. Slow. Don't use for regular browsing.

brave.title: Brave setup (2 min)
steps: Settings -> Privacy & security: enable aggressive tracker/ad blocking.
Turn on "Forget me when closing" for third-party cookies.
Disable Google services (autofill, web services you don’t need).

firefox.title: Firefox setup (3 min)
steps: Settings -> Privacy: choose "Strict".
Enable HTTPS-Only mode in all windows.
about:config -> set telemetry to false (toolkit.telemetry.enabled).

tor.title: Tor basics (2 min)
steps: Use for sensitive browsing only; avoid logging into personal accounts.
Keep Security Level at "Safer" or "Safest" for less fingerprinting.
Do not resize the window or install extensions.

social.title: Social Media & Messaging
social.subtitle: Secure your communications and protect your data on public networks.

e2e_explanation.title: What is End-to-End Encryption (E2EE)?
e2e_explanation.desc: Imagine sending a letter in a locked steel box. You have the key, and only the recipient has the key. The mailman (the app server) delivers the box but cannot open it. That is E2EE. Standard messaging is like a postcard—anyone handling it can read it.

signal.title: Signal - The Gold Standard
signal.desc: USE THIS. End-to-end encrypted, open source, non-profit. Even Signal cannot see your messages or who you talk to.

whatsapp.desc: Encrypted messages, but owned by Meta. Collects metadata (who you talk to, when, how often). Use Signal instead.

metadata.title: Metadata that apps keep
points: Signal: minimal (who you contact and when is protected).
WhatsApp/iMessage: metadata like who/when can be collected.
SMS: no encryption; assume everything is visible to carrier.

verification.title: Verify safety numbers/keys (Signal)
steps: Open chat -> tap name -> "View safety number".
Scan or compare digits with the person in real time.
Tap "Verified" so you get alerts if it changes (possible hijack).

vpn.title: VPN Services
vpn.intro: Use a VPN on public WiFi to encrypt your traffic and hide your IP address.
vpn.mullvad: USE THIS. Maximum privacy. No email needed—account is just a number. Flat €5/month. No tracking.
vpn.proton: Good free tier if you're in the Proton ecosystem. Swiss-based, no-logs.
vpn.ivpn: Privacy-focused alternative. No email required. Transparent company.

explanation.title: How does a VPN work?
explanation.desc: A VPN (Virtual Private Network) creates a secure 'tunnel' between your device and the internet. It hides your location (IP address) and encrypts your data so WiFi hackers or your ISP cannot see what websites you visit.

wifi.title: Do this on public Wi‑Fi
wifi.donts_title: Avoid doing this on public Wi‑Fi
items: Use a VPN before opening apps or sites.
Turn on HTTPS-Only in your browser.
Forget the network when done; turn off auto-join.
donts: No banking on unknown Wi‑Fi without a VPN.
Avoid installing apps/updates while on public Wi‑Fi.
Don't share files over AirDrop/Bluetooth unless needed.

email.title: Private Email
email.why: Gmail scans your emails for ads and shares data with Google. With Proton Mail, your emails are encrypted—even Proton can't read them.

proton.desc: USE THIS. Encrypted email based in Switzerland. Free tier available. Even Proton cannot read your emails.

gmail.desc: Google reads your emails to show you ads. Your data is used for profiling. Keep it for spam signups only.

devices.title: Device Security
devices.subtitle: Secure your mobile devices and desktop computers.
checklist_items: Enable screen lock (6-digit PIN or biometric)
Disable lock screen notifications for sensitive apps

ios_apps.title: iOS Apps
ios_apps.lockdown: Lockdown: Open source firewall and tracker blocker.

desktop_tools.title: Desktop Tools
desktop_tools.thunderbird: Thunderbird: Open source email client with PGP support.

resilience.title: Resilience checklist
items: Full-disk encryption on (FileVault, BitLocker, Android/iOS default).
Automatic cloud backups enabled (iCloud/Google Drive/OneDrive).
Set updates to automatic for OS and browser.

lost_device.title: If your device is lost/stolen
steps: Use Find My / Find My Device to lock and locate, then erase if unrecoverable.
Change passwords for email + banking first; revoke old sessions.
Notify your carrier (SIM swap risk) and your bank if applicable.

options: Protects data if the device is lost/stolen
questions.correct: Encryption keeps data unreadable without your key/PIN.
questions.explainer: Physical loss is common; encryption limits damage.

questions.prompt: What to do first if a phone is stolen?
options: Use Find My to lock/erase and change passwords for email/bank
questions.correct: Lock/erase remotely and secure key accounts immediately.
Off-device backups protect against loss, theft, or ransomware.
questions.explainer: Local-only backups are lost with the device.

phishing.subtitle: Don't take the bait. Learn to spot fake emails and scams.

urgency.title: Urgency
urgency.desc: Claims you must act immediately (e.g., 'Account suspended').

greeting.title: Generic Greeting
greeting.desc: Uses 'Dear Customer' instead of your name.

attachment.title: Unexpected Attachment
attachment.desc: Invoices or receipts you didn't ask for.

checklist.title: Email Security Checklist
items: Enable Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) on your email account.
Use a unique, strong password (generated by a password manager).
Never click links in suspicious emails. Go to the site directly.
Check the sender's actual email address, not just the display name.

tips.title: Micro-tips to stay safe
items: Hover or long-press links to reveal the real URL before clicking.
When in doubt, open a new tab and type the site yourself.
Unexpected invoices/attachments? Call the sender on a known number first.

sample.title: Example phishing email (what to notice)
sample.subject: Subject: URGENT - Account Suspended
sample.body: Hi, your account will be closed in 12 hours. Download the attached invoice or log in here.

after_click.title: If you already clicked
steps: Disconnect from Wi‑Fi; run an antivirus scan (desktop).
Change the password for the impacted site and enable MFA.
Revoke sessions/devices on that account; check recent activity.
If you entered credit card info, call the bank to block/replace the card.

questions.prompt: An email says your account will be closed in 1 hour and the button opens paypa1-support.com. What is the best action?
options: Hover, spot the fake domain, delete, then go directly to paypal.com
questions.correct: Right—never click, use a trusted URL you type yourself.
questions.explainer: Avoid engaging. Go direct to the real site or app.

questions.prompt: A coworker sends an unexpected invoice attachment. What’s safest?
options: Call/message them on a known channel to confirm before opening
questions.correct: Verification on a separate channel stops most phish attempts.
questions.explainer: Never open surprise attachments before confirming.

questions.prompt: You clicked a phishing link and entered credentials. What first?
options: Change that account’s password and enable MFA immediately
questions.correct: Resetting access + MFA is the most urgent step.
questions.explainer: Contain the account right away; then review activity.

encryption.title: How encryption protects you
encryption.intro: Think of encryption as a lock on your data. Without the key, it's unreadable gibberish.

items.name: One key (symmetric)
items.desc: Like a safe with one key. You lock your data, and only someone with the same key can open it. Your phone uses this to protect everything when locked.

items.name: Two keys (asymmetric)
items.desc: Like a mailbox: anyone can drop a letter in (public key), but only you have the key to open it (private key). This is how secure websites work.

items.name: Hashing (fingerprints)
items.desc: Creates a unique 'fingerprint' of data. Used to check if files are tampered with, and to store passwords safely—websites store the fingerprint, not your actual password.

items.name: E2E vs regular encryption
items.desc: Regular: like a sealed bag—the mail carrier can't read it in transit, but the post office (server) can open it. E2E: like a locked box inside the bag—only you and the recipient have keys.

takeaways: The tools we recommend (Signal, Bitwarden, Proton) handle encryption for you—just use them.
Never share recovery phrases or backup codes. Treat them like cash.
If your device is lost/stolen, change your passwords. The encryption key may be compromised.
Green padlock in browser = encrypted connection. Red warning = stop and don't proceed.
